video_title: Lawfare Daily: Purges and Power Plays in Domestic Ukrainian Politics
gist: Kyiv Independent reporter Danilo Mockrek argues Zilinski's firing of defense minister Federov was really about control of Ukraine's defense procurement budget, and that the ensuing purge - Serski out, Umeov parked atop foreign intelligence while keeping drone-deal and US/Russia negotiation portfolios, ambassador Ola Stefan sacked days before NABU charged her - is eroding the presidency's legitimacy rather than any one official's career. Federov's presidential rating roughly tripled to ~13% after the firing and Zilinski now loses every hypothetical second-round runoff, while shrinking protests signal citizens have given up on being heard rather than changed their minds.

themes.theme: Defense procurement as the real fight

insights.claim: The official reason given for firing Ukrainian defense minister Federov — his feud with armed forces chief Serski — is not credible, because Serski has since been fired too and protesters still demand Federov's return.
insights.speaker: Danilo Mockrek, guest (Kyiv Independent reporter)
insights.so_what: Treat Kyiv's stated personnel rationales as noise; the operative variable is control of the defense budget, which drives who wins Ukrainian defense contracts.
insights.quote: So if the conflict with Cerski was the only reason for firing him uh from from the defense ministry. So now this reason is is is gone.

insights.claim: Federov said in his only post-firing interview that his push to make Ukraine's multi-billion-dollar defense procurement transparent and data-driven — allocating contracts by what actually kills most Russians rather than by political influence — generated enough elite pushback to reach the president's door.
insights.speaker: Danilo Mockrek, guest (Kyiv Independent reporter)
insights.so_what: Politically connected incumbent suppliers keep their edge in Ukraine; performance-based procurement reform is stalled, a negative for merit-selected foreign and drone-tech vendors.
insights.quote: by what actually kills most Russians on the front line

insights.claim: Ukrainian law requires the defense minister and his deputies to be civilians under the NATO civilian-control standard, which structurally limits the president's ability to install generals and gives the civilian public a legitimate claim on the appointment.
insights.speaker: Danilo Mockrek, guest (Kyiv Independent reporter)
insights.so_what: Constrains the shortlist for a confirmed Ukrainian defense minister and explains why an ex-SBU general can only serve in an acting capacity.
insights.quote: in Ukrainian law the minister of defense is supposed to be a civilian and his deputies are are supposed to be civilians

themes.theme: Legitimacy vs legality under martial law

insights.claim: Zilinski is legally president — constitutional lawyers agree martial law extends the five-year mandate he won in 2019 — but legitimacy is a political rather than legal phenomenon, resting on a social consensus that he is protecting the country, and that consensus is eroding.
insights.speaker: Danilo Mockrek, guest (Kyiv Independent reporter)
insights.so_what: Legality is not the risk metric for Ukraine sovereign and reconstruction exposure; perceived legitimacy is, and it degrades with no legal event to flag it.

insights.claim: The weakening of the institution of the Ukrainian presidency during wartime, not Zilinski's personal political career, is what makes the current purges dangerous for Ukraine as a state.
insights.speaker: Danilo Mockrek, guest (Kyiv Independent reporter)
insights.so_what: Institutional erosion is the transmission channel from Kyiv palace politics to war-fighting capacity and Western aid confidence.
insights.quote: when I see the institution of president of Ukraine weakening

insights.claim: Zilinski has not held a large open press conference since February of last year — roughly eighteen months — gave time to Laura Loomer and Sky News during the protests while refusing every Ukrainian journalist, and did not acknowledge a roughly 50,000-person Kyiv march on July 31 in any address.
insights.speaker: Danilo Mockrek, guest (Kyiv Independent reporter)
insights.so_what: A leader communicating only to foreign audiences is optimizing for external aid flows over domestic consent — a fragile posture if aid politics turn.
insights.quote: He did find time for Laura Loomer. He did find time for Sky News during those protests, but he did not find any time for a Ukrainian journalist

insights.claim: Zilinski's recurring pattern is to offer official explanations nobody believes — the Serski conflict now, 'Russian influence' inside the anti-corruption agencies last year — which itself compounds the credibility loss.
insights.speaker: Danilo Mockrek, guest (Kyiv Independent reporter)
insights.so_what: Assume the stated rationale for any Kyiv personnel move is a decoy and price the unstated one.
insights.quote: He gives you an official explanation that just just doesn't sound plausible

themes.theme: Shrinking protests as a bearish signal

insights.claim: Ukraine's pro-Federov protests thinning out is bad news for Zilinski rather than good, because those who stopped coming did not lose faith in Federov or in protest — they lost faith in the president's willingness to hear them.
insights.speaker: Danilo Mockrek, guest (Kyiv Independent reporter)
insights.so_what: Crowd-size decay is a false all-clear; the political risk moves from the street into a permanently detached electorate.
insights.quote: The only thing they lost hope in was in President Zalinsk's ability and willingness to hear them.

insights.claim: Last year's reversal on dismantling Ukraine's anti-corruption infrastructure cost Zilinski nothing in the polls and actually boosted him by creating the image of a president who listens — the opposite of the current playbook.
insights.speaker: Danilo Mockrek, guest (Kyiv Independent reporter)
insights.so_what: A cheap de-escalation path is demonstrably available (reinstate Federov); its non-use signals the president is optimizing against weakness optics rather than ratings.

insights.claim: Firing armed forces chief Serski was a concession thrown to the street precisely because it did not require Zilinski to reverse his own decision on Federov, which he believes would make him look weak.
insights.speaker: Danilo Mockrek, guest (Kyiv Independent reporter)
insights.so_what: Expect further sacrificial firings of third parties rather than reversals — a template for reading future Kyiv concessions.

insights.claim: Federov's presidential polling rose from roughly 4-5% before his firing as Ukrainian defense minister to around 13% after it, with trust ratings far above Zilinski's.
insights.speaker: Danilo Mockrek, guest (Kyiv Independent reporter)
insights.so_what: The purge manufactured the strongest new opposition figure in Ukraine — a name to track for any eventual post-war political settlement.
insights.quote: his presidential rating right now is around 13%

insights.claim: The latest hypothetical Ukrainian polling shows Zilinski losing a second-round presidential runoff to the former top general now serving as ambassador in London, to Federov and to intelligence chief Budanov alike.
insights.speaker: Danilo Mockrek, guest (Kyiv Independent reporter)
insights.so_what: Any move toward wartime or post-war elections carries a high probability of leadership change in Kyiv — a discontinuity risk for negotiated-settlement scenarios.
insights.quote: Zalinski basically loses in in a second tour of presidential elections

insights.claim: The idea of holding Ukrainian elections late this year was driven by Zilinski's own favorable ratings trajectory rather than front-line stability or national interest, and scenarios are being actively game-planned inside the presidential office, including a reported not-so-secret meeting with senior figures such as the former top general now ambassador in London.
insights.speaker: Danilo Mockrek, guest (Kyiv Independent reporter)
insights.so_what: Read Ukrainian election-timing headlines as a real-time proxy for the president's internal polling, not as a signal about battlefield conditions.
insights.quote: the reasoning is when would it be best for me to have a presidential election

insights.claim: Federov rejected every alternative post offered to him, including vice prime minister for military technology, holding out for the defense ministry or nothing, because a vice premiership without a ministry carries no team, no policy-enforcement power and no real leverage.
insights.speaker: Danilo Mockrek, guest (Kyiv Independent reporter)
insights.so_what: Title inflation is Kyiv's standard tool for defusing protest without ceding control; separate coordinator roles from budget-holding ministries when assessing who actually decides.
insights.quote: having a position does not mean having real power

insights.claim: Federov appears to want the defense ministry back rather than a presidential run, and the guest judges that return will not happen.
insights.speaker: Danilo Mockrek, guest (Kyiv Independent reporter)
insights.so_what: A blocked but popular Federov remains a latent political force outside government — an overhang on Zilinski's authority for as long as the war lasts.

insights.claim: Zilinski's personnel method works like a box of about thirty puzzle pieces he keeps forcing into different pictures — the same loyalists rotated through unrelated institutions by fit-to-person rather than fit-to-job.
insights.speaker: Danilo Mockrek, guest (Kyiv Independent reporter)
insights.so_what: A reusable model for forecasting Kyiv appointments: predict from the roster of protected insiders, not from institutional needs or CVs.
insights.quote: Like President Zilinski has a box of say uh 30 puzzles, okay?

insights.claim: Umeov, whose name appears on the leaked corruption recordings referred to in the episode as the 'mindage tapes', was made interim head of Ukraine's foreign intelligence service while explicitly keeping his portfolios on negotiations with the US and Russia and on drone deals with partners — tasks outside that agency's remit.
insights.speaker: Anastasia Patina, host (Lawfare Ukraine fellow)
insights.so_what: Ukraine's counterparty on drone procurement and US/Russia talks is now an intelligence chief with an unrelated brief and corruption exposure — a due-diligence flag for anyone contracting into that channel.
insights.quote: making drone deals is not actually part of the job of the head of a, you know, foreign intelligence service

insights.claim: The Ukrainian reshuffle chain placed people before functions: Klymenko was pulled out of the interior ministry to become defense minister, that plan collapsed amid protests and parliamentary arithmetic, so Umeov was displaced from secretary of the National Security and Defense Council to create a landing spot for Klymenko.
insights.speaker: Danilo Mockrek, guest (Kyiv Independent reporter)
insights.so_what: Shows Ukrainian security-sector leadership being allocated as a patronage clearing problem, so institutional continuity cannot be assumed in any counterparty relationship.
insights.quote: It does not have a real state logic in it

insights.claim: Ukraine's acting defense minister is the former head of the SBU, the SBU is now run on an interim basis by his first deputy Alexander Pled, and three posts — defense, foreign affairs and the SBU — require parliamentary votes while the foreign intelligence service does not, leaving Umeov secure in his job.
insights.speaker: Danilo Mockrek, guest (Kyiv Independent reporter)
insights.so_what: Maps exactly where the Ukrainian parliament retains leverage over the security apparatus and where the president can act unilaterally.
insights.quote: the parliament's intervention is not required

insights.claim: Ukraine's parliament went into a month-long recess the day after Federov's firing and returns on August 18 into a planned pro-Federov protest, but even if it cannot muster votes for the nominated defense minister he simply stays on as acting minister, and Zilinski is not expected to budge.
insights.speaker: Danilo Mockrek, guest (Kyiv Independent reporter)
insights.so_what: Watch August 18 as the next catalyst date, but expect institutional stalemate — indefinite 'acting' leadership — rather than resolution.
insights.quote: he would just remain acting minister of defense

themes.theme: Stefan case and Ukraine's corruption tolerance line

insights.claim: Ukraine's ambassador to the US, Ola Stefan, was dismissed without explanation on August 3 and charged by NABU three days later with illicit enrichment and false asset declarations, including two Kyiv apartments bought through a friend with undeclared money; both events had been rumored two weeks in advance, suggesting the firing was timed to pre-empt the charges.
insights.speaker: Anastasia Patina, host (Lawfare Ukraine fellow)
insights.so_what: Kyiv rumor flow ran two weeks ahead of both the sacking and the indictment — a usable lead indicator for Ukrainian personnel and legal events.
insights.quote: Both proved proved right. Proved true.

insights.claim: Stefan's older Ukrainian corruption case involves a Ministry of Justice procurement about thirteen years ago under Yanukovich in which taxpayers paid over $300,000 for low-quality comparative analyses of Ukrainian and EU law that Ukrainian universities had offered to produce for free, with contracts going to inexperienced companies whose delivery she signed off on.
insights.speaker: Danilo Mockrek, guest (Kyiv Independent reporter)
insights.so_what: A concrete template for how EU-integration technical-assistance budgets get siphoned — relevant to any donor or lender funding Ukraine's legal approximation work.

insights.claim: Stefan was served a notice of suspicion in 2019 and became a defendant in Ukraine's high anti-corruption court, yet was still appointed vice prime minister for European integration in 2020, then justice minister — the very ministry her case concerns — and later ambassador to Washington.
insights.speaker: Danilo Mockrek, guest (Kyiv Independent reporter)
insights.so_what: An active indictment is no bar to top Ukrainian office, so anti-corruption case flow is a weak predictor of who holds power.

insights.claim: Appointing suspects or figures named in corruption cases is routine in Ukraine rather than exceptional, and the guest argues that the narrative treating hundreds of thousands of dollars as merely 'minor' corruption does more damage to Ukraine than the corrupt officials themselves.
insights.speaker: Danilo Mockrek, guest (Kyiv Independent reporter)
insights.so_what: The tolerance threshold, not the case count, determines whether Ukraine's anti-corruption architecture ever bites — a core variable for EU accession timelines and donor conditionality.
insights.quote: you have to promote zero tolerance for corruption to have at least a chance to fight it to a decent level

insights.claim: The next Ukrainian ambassador to the US is undecided: the former prime minister was tapped first but reportedly refused, Umeov was rumored, and Pisa — deputy head of Zilinski's presidential office, whom Trump complimented at their last meeting — has since been floated.
insights.speaker: Anastasia Patina, host (Lawfare Ukraine fellow)
insights.so_what: Whoever lands the Washington post signals whether Kyiv is optimizing the US channel for Trump-personal rapport or for institutional competence.
